title: How to Waterproof a Basement: 7 Steps, Cheapest Fix First
h1: How to Waterproof a Basement: DIY Basement Waterproofing in 7 Steps
keywords: how to waterproof a basement floor
description: Waterproof a basement in 5 steps from the outside in: gutters and downspouts first (often $20 to $300), then grading, crack sealing, wall coating and drains.
dek: Waterproof a basement in 5 steps from the outside in: gutters and downspouts first (often $20 to $300), then grading, crack sealing, wall coating and drains.
intro: To waterproof a basement, work from the outside in: move roof water away with clean gutters and long downspout extensions, slope the soil away from the walls, seal cracks and pipe holes, coat walls that still seep, and add an interior drain with a sump pump only if water keeps coming in at the floor. The first two steps usually cost $20 to a few hundred dollars and fix more wet basements than any product sold for the inside.

This guide walks through all seven steps in the order water reaches your foundation, with the rough cost of each, which ones you can do yourself, and the signs that mean you need a contractor or an engineer instead. It is built from coating data sheets, manufacturer installation instructions, the International Residential Code and common contractor practice, not from a sales pitch for one system.
quickAnswer: The best way to waterproof a basement is to stop water before it reaches the concrete. Extend every downspout at least 4 to 6 feet and regrade so the soil drops about 6 inches over the first 10 feet. Then seal cracks, coat damp walls with a masonry waterproofer, and save interior drain tile ($5,000 to $15,000) or exterior excavation ($15,000 to $30,000 or more) for water that still gets in.

sections.h: How to Waterproof a Basement: DIY Basement Waterproofing in 7 Steps at a Glance

blocks.p: **Short answer:** basement waterproofing works in layers. The outer layer (roof water and grading) decides how much water reaches the foundation. The middle layer (the concrete itself) decides how much gets through. The inner layer (an interior drain and sump pump) catches whatever is left. Each layer is cheaper than the one inside it, so fix them in that order and you only pay for the expensive work if the cheap work fails.

blocks.p: Costs are the ranges contractors and suppliers commonly quote; your house, region and access change them. The point of the table is the order. Most people do it backward: they see a wet wall, buy a coating, and only look at the downspouts after the coating blisters.

If your basement only feels clammy and musty in summer and never gets wet after rain, you may not need waterproofing at all. That is usually humidity, and our guide on [how to fix a damp basement](/how-to-fix-a-damp-basement/) covers the dehumidifier side of the problem.

sections.h: Where Is the Water in Your Basement Coming From?

blocks.p: Every waterproofing decision depends on one fact: where the water enters. Spend a day finding it before you spend money fixing it.

blocks.h3: Map the wet spots during a storm

blocks.p: Go down with a flashlight during or right after a hard rain. Put a strip of painter's tape beside every wet area and write the date on it. Note the exact location of each one: the face of the wall, a crack, a form-tie hole, the seam where wall meets floor, the middle of the slab, or around a window, pipe or wire. A rough sketch of the basement with those marks is the most useful thing you can hand a contractor, and it often shows you that every wet spot sits under the same downspout.

blocks.h3: Run a hose test when it will not rain

blocks.p: Lay a garden hose at the base of the foundation outside and let it run gently for 20 to 30 minutes while someone watches inside. Start at the soil line under the suspect area, then move to the window well, then to the downspout outlet. When water appears inside, you have found the path. It is slow, but it replaces guesswork with evidence.

Tape a square of clear plastic, about 18 inches on a side, tight to the bare wall and leave it for a day or two. Water on the room side of the plastic is humid air condensing on cool concrete. Water between the plastic and the wall is moisture coming through the masonry. Only the second one is a waterproofing problem.

blocks.p: The cove joint deserves extra attention. The wall and the floor were poured at different times, so the seam between them is never truly bonded. When the soil around the footing is soaked, water rises through that seam, and no paint or coating on the wall can stop it.

sections.h: How Do You Keep Roof Water Away From the Foundation?

blocks.p: This is the cheapest basement waterproofing there is, and it fixes more leaks than anything else on this page.

blocks.h3: Why roof water matters so much

blocks.p: A roof collects a startling amount of rain. Put an inch of rain on a 1,500 square foot roof and you have roughly 900 gallons of water, almost all of it routed through a handful of downspouts. If a downspout empties at the foot of the wall, it soaks the soil in exactly the spot where it does the most harm, and that patch of saturated soil presses water against the foundation every storm.

Clear leaves and grit, then run a hose in the far end of each run. Water should flow steadily toward the downspout. Standing water means the gutter has lost its slope and will overflow along the house; overflow lands right beside the foundation, the same as a short downspout.

Get the water at least 4 feet from the foundation, and 6 to 10 feet on clay soil or where the yard tips toward the house. Rigid aluminum or vinyl extensions, flexible corrugated pipe, roll-out sleeves and splash blocks all work, as long as the water lands on ground that keeps running away from the house. Extensions that flip up for mowing are fine if someone remembers to flip them back down.

Underground drain pipes look tidy and fail without any sign at the surface. Clay and thin corrugated lines crack, sag and fill with roots and silt. Run a hose into each one and make sure the water comes out freely at the far end. A blocked buried line dumps the whole roof's water next to the footing, which is the worst possible outcome. If it does not flow, disconnect it and use an above-ground extension until it is dug up and replaced.

After you change the roof drainage, give it two or three real storms before doing anything else. Many basements that looked like they needed a drain system go dry once the downspouts are moved. If water still appears, you have lost nothing, and whatever you install next will have less water to handle.

sections.h: How Should the Ground Slope Around a Basement?

blocks.p: Soil next to the house should fall away from the foundation. Where the lot permits, the International Residential Code wants the ground to fall a minimum of 6 inches across the first 10 feet out from the wall. Over the years backfill settles, mulch and planting beds build up, and that slope flattens or reverses until rain runs straight to the wall.

Lay a straight 8 to 10 foot board on the ground running out from the wall, set a level on it, and lift the far end until the bubble centers. The gap under the far end tells you the fall. If the board has to be lifted at the house end instead, the ground slopes toward you.

blocks.h3: Rebuild it with the right soil

blocks.p: Build up low areas with topsoil that has some clay in it; sand, gravel and mulch let rain soak straight down beside the wall, while clay sheds it outward. Add it in thin layers and tamp each one. Stop the new soil a good 6 inches short of the siding and any wood, or you trade a wet basement for rot and termite trouble. Cover it with grass or a thin mulch layer, not a deep bed that holds water against the wall.

A window well is a hole dug next to your foundation, so it needs its own drainage. The bottom should be a few inches below the window sill, filled with several inches of gravel or tied to a drain. The liner should be sealed tight to the wall. A clear well cover keeps out rain and leaves while letting in light. A well that holds a puddle against a basement window will eventually leak through it.

blocks.h3: Look for small steady water sources

blocks.p: Walk the house and look for anything that keeps one patch of soil wet: a sprinkler head hitting the foundation, an air conditioner condensate line dripping at the wall, a patio or walkway that tips toward the house, or a hose bib that drips. These cost little to fix and remove a constant supply of water that coatings and drains would otherwise have to fight.

sections.h: How Do You Seal Basement Wall Cracks and Holes Yourself?

blocks.p: Poured concrete walls almost always have a few shrinkage cracks, and most are not structural. They are, however, ideal water paths. Sealing them is the main DIY step for the middle layer of waterproofing.

The standard DIY repair is an injection kit. You glue plastic ports along the crack every 8 to 12 inches, seal the surface of the crack between the ports with an epoxy paste, and then push liquid resin into the lowest port until it appears at the next one up. You cap that port and move up the crack. The goal is to fill the crack through the full thickness of the wall, not just the surface.

ul: **Polyurethane** is the usual choice for a leaking crack. It foams, expands to fill voids, and stays slightly flexible, so it tolerates small seasonal movement.
**Epoxy** cures hard and bonds the two sides of the crack together. That is useful for a structural repair an engineer has signed off on, but it is less forgiving on a crack that still moves.

blocks.p: Kits commonly treat several feet of crack, and the prep matters more than the brand: the crack must be clean, and the surface paste must fully cure before you inject.

If water is actively flowing from a crack or a form-tie hole, inject nothing yet. Chisel the opening into a slight undercut, mix hydraulic cement stiff, press it in and hold it for a few minutes while it sets and swells. That stops the flow so you can treat the area properly later. It is a plug, not a full-depth repair.
Seal every penetration through the wall, such as water lines, gas lines, cable and dryer vents, with a urethane sealant or a foam rated for foundations, from inside and outside where you can reach.

blocks.h3: When to stop and call an engineer

blocks.p: Leave these alone until an engineer has seen them: cracks running sideways, cracks stepping up through block mortar joints, anything wider than roughly a quarter inch, and walls that lean in. Those point to soil pushing on the wall. Sealing them hides the evidence while the force keeps working, and the right repair may be wall anchors or bracing rather than resin.

sections.h: How Do You Waterproof Basement Walls From the Inside?

blocks.p: With the downspouts sorted and the cracks filled, walls that still darken or feel damp after a storm are candidates for a coating. Interior coatings are the most popular basement waterproofing technique and also the most oversold, so it helps to know what they can and cannot do.

blocks.p: Our ranking of the [best basement wall sealers](/best-basement-wall-sealer/) compares specific products by the kind of moisture each handles, and the [best cinder block sealers](/best-cinder-block-sealer-reviews/) guide covers hollow block, which behaves differently from solid poured concrete.

Wire-brush off old paint, efflorescence (the white chalky crust) and loose material. Wash the wall with a masonry cleaner, rinse it, and let it dry. Coatings need bare masonry to bond; a waterproofer brushed over old paint only waterproofs the paint.

blocks.h3: Apply it the way the label says

blocks.p: Most masonry waterproofers want a stiff brush for the first coat, worked hard in several directions until every pinhole on a block wall is filled. Rolling a first coat onto block leaves pinholes that wick water. Apply the second coat after the label's dry time. Two full coats almost always beat one heavy one.

blocks.h3: What a wall coating will not do

blocks.p: A coating slows seepage and dampness through the face of the wall. It does not stop water rising through the cove joint, it will not hold back a flowing leak, and it can blister if strong water pressure builds behind it. If the walls stay dry after coating but water still collects along the floor edge, the next step is drainage, not another coat. If you plan to paint the walls for looks afterward, use a coating listed as paintable or follow our [best paint for cinder block](/best-paint-for-cinder-block/) guide.

sections.h: How Do You Waterproof a Basement Floor?

blocks.p: A basement floor gets wet in three different ways, and each has its own fix.

blocks.h3: Water at the edge of the floor

blocks.p: Water that appears along the wall-floor seam after storms is coming up through the cove joint from saturated soil. Caulking the seam rarely holds, because the water simply finds the next weak point. The fix is outside drainage first, then an interior perimeter drain if water still collects.

blocks.h3: Water in the middle of the slab

blocks.p: Water that wells up through cracks in the middle of the floor usually means a high water table or water pressure under the slab. Seal small cracks if you like, but expect an interior drain with a sump pump to be the real answer, sometimes with extra drain lines under the slab.

A slab that feels cool and damp, darkens under a rug, or fails the plastic sheet test is passing water vapor up from the soil. Many older slabs were poured without a vapor barrier. A penetrating sealer can reduce that vapor on bare concrete, and a dehumidifier handles what reaches the air.

blocks.h3: Paint is a finish, not a waterproofer

blocks.p: Basement floor paint will not stop water, and a dense coating on a damp slab blisters. If you want a painted floor, waterproof first, prove the slab stays dry through a wet season, then follow our guide to the [best basement floor paint](/best-basement-floor-paint/), which matches breathable and epoxy products to slab moisture.

blocks.h3: Floors you can live with on a borderline slab

blocks.p: If the floor is dry enough to use but not perfect, choose finishes that tolerate it: luxury vinyl plank with a waterproof core over a vapor-retarding underlayment, ceramic or porcelain tile, or sealed concrete. Wall-to-wall carpet with a pad is the worst choice, because it hides water and feeds mold.

sections.h: When Do You Need Interior Drain Tile and a Sump Pump?

blocks.p: An interior perimeter drain is the standard fix when water keeps coming in at the floor even after the outside work is done. It does not stop water reaching the foundation. It catches the water under the slab and pumps it out before it reaches your floor.

The installer cuts out a band of floor along the inside of each exterior wall, excavates next to the footing, beds perforated drain pipe in clean stone, and pitches the whole run toward a sump pit. A dimpled plastic membrane is often run up the wall behind the trench so water that weeps through the wall drops into the drain too. The slab is then patched with new concrete.

ul: A **1/3 horsepower** submersible pump handles most houses; homes with a high water table or a large drain area may need **1/2 horsepower**.
For longevity, most installers favor a cast-iron pump with a mechanical float rather than an electronic switch.
The discharge line should carry water 10 to 20 feet from the house onto ground that drains away, not back to the foundation.
A **battery backup pump** in the same pit, or at least a high-water alarm, matters because power failures arrive with the same storms that fill the pit.

blocks.p: Our ranking of [basement waterproofing systems](/best-basement-waterproofing-systems/) compares specific pumps, backups and crack kits.

blocks.h3: What it costs and what to ask

blocks.p: Interior drain systems are commonly quoted at $5,000 to $15,000 installed, depending on wall length, slab thickness and access. Get at least three quotes. Ask each contractor to show you where they think the water enters, what the warranty covers (the pump, the drain, or a dry basement), and who pulls the permit. A good contractor asks about your gutters and grading before quoting a drain.

It is possible with a rented concrete saw, a demolition hammer, a lot of stone and a strong back, but it is heavy, dusty, hard to undo, and easy to get wrong at the sump. The practical DIY job is upgrading an existing pump, adding a battery backup or a high-water alarm, and testing the system twice a year by filling the pit with a bucket.

sections.h: Is Exterior Basement Waterproofing Worth the Cost?

blocks.p: Exterior waterproofing is the most complete fix and by far the most expensive. The foundation is dug out to the footing on the outside, the wall is cleaned and patched, a membrane goes on, drainage board covers it, a perforated drain is laid along the footing, and the trench is refilled with gravel that lets water drop to that drain. Water then meets the membrane and drains away before it touches the concrete.

ul: The foundation needs structural work from the outside anyway, such as bowing walls or failed block.
The soil around the house stays soaked for long periods, so an interior drain would run almost constantly.
You are already digging for an addition, a new sewer line or a foundation repair, so the excavation cost is partly paid.
The leak trace points clearly at one wall, so a partial dig on that side is enough.

blocks.p: Full-perimeter exterior work is commonly quoted at $15,000 to $30,000 or more, and decks, patios, driveways and landscaping that must be removed push it higher. A single problem wall costs a fraction of that, which is why the tracing in the first step pays for itself.

Ask which membrane they use, whether they add drainage board over it, and where the footing drain empties. A footing drain has to go somewhere: to daylight on a sloping lot or to a sump. A membrane with no working drain just holds water against the wall, which defeats the point of digging.

Exterior is better engineering because it keeps water off the wall entirely. Interior drainage is the common compromise because it costs much less and works on any lot. For many homes the honest answer is neither: once gutters, grading and cracks are handled, there is nothing left for a system to catch.

sections.h: What Is the Cheapest Way to Waterproof a Basement?

blocks.p: The cheapest way to waterproof a basement is to control roof water and grading. Those two steps together often cost under a few hundred dollars and a couple of weekends, and they address the most common causes of basement leaks.

blocks.p: For many houses the full DIY sequence stays under about $1,000 and runs over a month or two, mostly because you wait for rain to judge each change.

blocks.h3: Plan the wall coating as the longest step

blocks.p: Expect four separate days: one to empty and scrub the walls, one to patch and let things dry, and one for each coat. Work one wall at a time if the basement is in use.

Leave the studs, drywall and carpet in the store until the basement has made it through a whole wet season without water. Keep notes and dated photos of what you did. If you sell the house, a clear record of drainage work and several dry seasons reassures buyers and inspectors far more than fresh paint.

blocks.h3: Why the cheap steps protect the expensive ones

blocks.p: Even when you do need a drain system, the outside work still pays off. A sump pump that cycles a few times per storm lasts longer than one that runs every few minutes because a downspout is dumping beside the pit.

sections.h: Can You Finish a Basement After Waterproofing It?

blocks.p: Yes, once it has stayed dry through a full wet season and the humidity stays under control. Finishing too early is the most expensive basement mistake, because drywall and carpet hide water until mold has already started.

Keep a cheap hygrometer in the basement and aim for 45 to 50 percent relative humidity in summer, with a [basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) if needed. Watch for new efflorescence, tide lines or damp spots after heavy rain and spring thaw. A year of clean readings is the best evidence you will get.

blocks.h3: Why water bubbles behind basement insulation

blocks.p: Owners often find water beading or bubbling behind plastic sheeting or foil-faced insulation on basement walls. That is usually one of two things: moisture coming through the concrete and trapped by the plastic, or warm room air sneaking behind the insulation and condensing on the cold wall. Either way the fix is the same. Remove plastic sheeting placed directly against fiberglass batts on a concrete wall, solve any seepage from outside, and use rigid foam board glued tight to the concrete with taped seams, which keeps the wall surface warm and has no hidden air gap.

ul: Rigid foam insulation against the concrete, not fiberglass batts behind a plastic vapor barrier.
Pressure-treated bottom plates where wood touches concrete, with a sill gasket under them.
A small gap between the bottom of the drywall and the floor.
Flooring that tolerates moisture, such as vinyl plank, tile or sealed concrete.
An access panel at the sump and at any wall you have had trouble with.

blocks.h3: Deal with any mold before you cover it

blocks.p: Clean small patches of growth on hard surfaces before framing, using a product from our [best mold remover](/best-mold-remover/) guide and proper protection, and replace moldy porous materials. If the space stays musty after it is dry, an [air purifier for mold](/best-air-purifier-for-mold/) with real carbon can help while you track down the source.

mistakes: Painting the walls before tracing the leak

A wall coating is the most visible fix, so it usually comes first. When the real entry point is the floor seam, a crack in the slab or a downspout pouring beside the foundation, paint on the wall cannot help, and it may bubble off. Spend an afternoon with a hose and a flashlight, find the entry point, and fix what the trace shows before buying any product.
Assuming buried downspout lines still drain

Underground downspout pipes crack and clog with roots and silt without any sign at the surface, and when they fail they deliver the roof's water straight to the footing. Run a hose into every buried line and confirm it flows out freely at the far end. If it does not, switch to an above-ground extension until the line is replaced.
Sealing a horizontal crack or a bowing wall

Horizontal cracks, stair-step cracks in block, and walls that lean inward are signs of soil pressure on the structure, not just a water path. Injecting or patching them hides the evidence while the pressure keeps working. Have a structural engineer look first; the right repair may be anchors or bracing, and waterproofing follows afterward.
Finishing the basement before it proves dry

Framing, drywall and carpet trap moisture and feed mold, and you will not see the problem until it smells. Wait until the basement stays dry through at least one full wet season after your fixes, then finish with rigid foam against the concrete, pressure-treated plates and moisture-tolerant flooring.
Relying on one sump pump with no backup

The storms that fill a sump pit fastest are the same ones that knock out power. A single pump on household current leaves the basement unprotected at the worst moment. Put a battery-powered backup pump in the pit, or at minimum a high-water alarm, and check them every few months by dumping a bucket of water in.
bottomLine: To waterproof a basement, follow the water: roof, soil, concrete, then the basement itself. Clean gutters and long downspout extensions come first and cost the least, regrading comes next, then crack injection and a properly brushed masonry coating. Only if water still comes in at the floor do you need an interior drain with a battery-backed sump pump, and only structural problems or a soaked lot usually justify digging up the outside. Keep notes, wait a full wet season, and the basement you finish will stay dry.

faqs.q: What is the best way to waterproof a basement?
faqs.a: The best way is to work from the outside in. Clean the gutters, extend downspouts 4 to 10 feet, and slope the soil away from the walls first. Then seal cracks and pipe holes, coat walls that still seep, and add an interior drain with a sump pump only if water keeps entering at the floor. Exterior excavation is the most thorough fix but is usually reserved for structural problems or very wet lots.

faqs.q: Can you waterproof a basement yourself?
faqs.a: Yes, most of it. Gutter and downspout work, regrading, crack injection and wall coatings are all reasonable do-it-yourself jobs with basic tools. Upgrading a sump pump or adding a battery backup is a one-afternoon project. Installing an interior perimeter drain is possible but heavy and hard to undo, and exterior excavation is contractor work. Doing the cheap outside steps first often makes the rest unnecessary.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to waterproof a basement?
faqs.a: Managing roof water is the cheapest fix. Clean the gutters and extend every downspout so it empties several feet from the foundation onto ground that slopes away, which typically costs $20 to $300. Correcting the grading next to the house is the next cheapest step. Both should come before any coating, drain or pump, because they address the most common cause of basement leaks.

faqs.q: Does waterproofing paint work on basement walls?
faqs.a: It works for dampness and slow seepage through the face of the wall when it is brushed onto clean, bare masonry in two full coats. It does not stop water entering at the wall-floor seam, it will not hold back a flowing crack, and it can blister under strong water pressure. Use it after the outdoor drainage fixes, not as a substitute for them.

faqs.q: Is interior or exterior basement waterproofing better?
faqs.a: Exterior waterproofing is better engineering because the membrane meets the water before it reaches the concrete, but it requires excavation and is commonly quoted at $15,000 to $30,000 or more. Interior drain tile with a sump pump, typically $5,000 to $15,000, is the common compromise: it collects water and pumps it out. Many homes need neither once gutters, grading and cracks are fixed.

faqs.q: How do you waterproof an existing basement floor?
faqs.a: Start by finding how the water arrives. Water along the wall-floor seam or welling through slab cracks needs outside drainage and, if it continues, an interior perimeter drain with a sump pump. A slab that is only damp from vapor can be treated with a penetrating concrete sealer and a dehumidifier. Floor paint is a finish, not a waterproofer, and should go on only after the slab stays dry.

faqs.q: How long does basement waterproofing last?
faqs.a: It depends on the method. Gutter and grading fixes last as long as you maintain them. Polyurethane crack injections often last decades. Masonry coatings commonly go five to ten years before touch-ups. Interior drain systems can last for decades, though sump pumps typically need replacing every 7 to 10 years. A well-installed exterior membrane is generally expected to last about as long as the foundation.
